title: Six animals
hook: a snake, crocodile, bird, dog, jackal and monkey tied to one post: the body as the post (SN 35.247)

segments.voice: Yesterday: kayagata sati, and your line, don't spill. Did you carry one full cup slowly, and notice how the whole body had to pay attention? Day three hundred ninety-two, the end of the week.

A man walks into a clearing with six animals on six ropes. A snake. A crocodile. A bird. A dog. A jackal. A monkey. He knots the six ropes together in the middle, and lets go. You can guess what happens next. The snake heads for its anthill. The crocodile heads for the river. The bird heads for the sky, the dog for the village, the jackal for the charnel ground, the monkey for the forest. Six directions, one knot, and whoever is strongest drags the rest. If you've ever opened your phone to check one thing and surfaced forty minutes later, you've met this knot. Today: the six animals, and the post.
screen: `SIX ANIMALS, SIX ROPES.` → `SIX DIRECTIONS, ONE KNOT.` → `THE STRONGEST DRAGS THE REST.`

segments.voice: The story comes from the Connected Discourses, in the book on the six senses. The Buddha tells it twice. The first time, the ropes are only tied to each other. Each animal pulls toward its own place, and the others get dragged after whichever is strongest. Then he tells it again with a single change. This time the man ties all six ropes to a strong post, driven deep into the ground. The animals pull just as hard. The snake still wants its anthill. The monkey still wants its forest. Nobody has been tamed. But the post doesn't move. And after a while, worn out, they stand by the post, then sit down by it, then lie down beside it. Then he explains. The six animals are the six senses: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body and mind, each pulling toward what it likes and away from what it doesn't. The post is mindfulness directed to the body, kayagata sati in Pali: knowing you're sitting while you sit, knowing you're breathing while you breathe. Notice what the Buddha doesn't say. He doesn't say kill the animals, or blindfold the eye, or stop up the ear. The senses keep their nature. The snake is still a snake. What changes is that there's something steady for all of them to be tied to. That's why this story belongs under right mindfulness, the seventh factor of the path. Mindfulness here isn't a mood. It's a post. Some teachers put it this way: the body is always here, and it's the mind that runs off to the anthill and the forest. Coming back to the feet on the floor is coming back to the post. And it's the end of a week: waking the good, keeping it going, the lute string tuned, remembering to notice, the gatekeeper, the bowl of oil, and today, six animals with something to be tied to.
screen: `TIED ONLY TO EACH OTHER.` · `THE SAME ANIMALS, TIED TO A POST.` · `SIX ANIMALS, SIX SENSES.` · `THE POST: MINDFULNESS OF THE BODY.` · then, large: `THE POST HOLDS.`

segments.voice: Sit, and find the post first. Feel your feet, the weight of your body on the seat, your hands where they rest. Then let the animals pull. A sound will tug at the ear. A thought will drag toward tomorrow. An itch will call from somewhere. You don't have to stop any of them. Just notice which one is pulling, and come back to the weight of the body. A pull, and back to the post. Another pull, and back. By the end, some of them may be lying down. The bell holds the time.
Six animals. The six senses, each pulling toward its own place, tied to one steady post: mindfulness of the body.
Your line: the post holds. Today, when something drags your attention away, feel your feet on the ground for one breath before you follow it. Day three hundred ninety-two.

howItsDone: Many Buddhists practice mindfulness of the body by returning attention to posture and breath through the day, in walking as well as sitting meditation; teachers in several schools describe the body as an anchor for the wandering mind.

match.prompt: match each animal to where it pulls, or what it stands for.

myth: in the story, the Buddha says to get rid of the six animals
the animals keep their nature; tied to a post, they pull until they tire and lie down.
the six animals stand for the six senses, including the mind
eye, ear, nose, tongue, body and mind: each pulls toward its own range.
tied only to each other, the animals end up following the strongest
that's the first telling; the second adds the post.

fork.setup: you've tied six animals to a strong post driven deep into the ground. they pull in six directions. what happens, in the Buddha's story?
options: they pull, tire, and lie down beside the post
the strongest drags the others away
fork.reveal: the post doesn't move. worn out, the animals stand, then sit, then lie down beside it. the senses aren't destroyed; they're given something steady.

original.note: Pali saḷāyatana: the six sense bases, eye, ear, nose, tongue, body and mind, which the six animals stand for.

trapdoor: what you thought: a list of animals to make a point about distraction.
what it means: six senses, each with its own pull, and one steady post that lets them settle.

what a scholar hears: the post is named kāyagatā sati, mindfulness directed to the body; the sutta is numbered SN 35.247 in Bhikkhu Bodhi's edition and SN 35.206 in the older Pali Text Society numbering.
recall: a Chan master who kept working

sources.ref: Samyutta Nikaya 35.247 (Chappana Sutta, the simile of the six animals)
Majjhima Nikaya 119, Kayagatasati Sutta (mindfulness of the body)

notes: The outline says 'the body as the post'; the sutta itself names the post as mindfulness directed to the body (kayagata sati). The script follows the sutta.
Animal destinations (anthill, water, sky, village, charnel ground, forest) given from memory of SN 35.247; please confirm.
Sutta numbering: SN 35.247 (Bodhi) / SN 35.206 (PTS) stated in the trapdoor; please confirm.

Editor review (2026-10-01): first telling corrected (the animals follow the strongest; exhaustion belongs to the post telling); 'the body is always in the present' now attributed to some teachers; original changed from kāyagatā sati (repeated from day 391) to saḷāyatana, the six sense bases.
